prompt: What separates continuous delivery from continuous deployment?

choices.text: Whether the tests run on every push
choices.why: Both run them; that is integration.

choices.text: Who puts a release into production, and when
choices.why: Right. A person chooses in delivery; it goes on its own in deployment.

choices.text: Whether there is a staging environment
choices.why: Either can have one.

choices.text: How many times a day the team deploys
choices.why: Frequency follows from the choice; it does not define it.

prompt: A team can release any green commit within the hour but chooses to release on Thursdays. What does it practise?

choices.text: Continuous deployment
choices.why: A person chooses the moment, so it is not deployment.

choices.text: Neither, because it waits
choices.why: Waiting by choice is allowed; needing a week to prepare is not.

choices.text: Continuous delivery
choices.why: Right. Releasing is routine; when is a decision.

choices.text: Only continuous integration
choices.why: It also has a deployable release at all times.

prompt: Order the practices from the one that promises least to the one that promises most.
trap: Delivery adds a deployable release; deployment removes the person from the last step.

prompt: Why build the artifact once instead of once per environment?

choices.text: To save disk space on the runner
choices.why: Space is not the argument.

choices.text: So production runs exactly what was tested
choices.why: Right. A second build is a second thing nobody tested.

choices.text: Because git archive can only run once per tag
choices.why: It runs as often as you like.

choices.text: Because production has no compiler
choices.why: shipquote is not compiled; the argument is about sameness.

prompt: The artifact was deleted and built again from the same commit. What did its SHA-256 do?

choices.text: Changed, because the build time differs
choices.why: git archive uses the commit's time, not the clock.

choices.text: Stayed the same
choices.why: Right. The build is reproducible.

choices.text: Changed only in its last characters
choices.why: A hash changes completely or not at all.

choices.text: Could not be computed a second time
choices.why: It was printed both times.

prompt: A build that gives the same bytes from the same commit every time is called ___ .
Where is shipquote's version written?

choices.text: In pyproject.toml, by hand before each release
choices.why: pyproject says version 0 and is never edited for a release.

choices.text: In the git tag, and nowhere else
choices.why: Right. The build stamps it into the artifact.

choices.text: In a constant in version.py
choices.why: version.py reads a stamped file, or says dev.

choices.text: In the deploy script's arguments
choices.why: The deploy reads it from the artifact's name.

prompt: What did the build call the commit one past v1.4.0 with no tag of its own?

choices.why: Nobody tagged 1.4.1; inventing it would be a lie.
That would let a different commit pass for the release.
Right. Not a release, and still exactly which commit.

choices.text: latest
choices.why: latest names nothing in particular.

prompt: Match each kind of release to the part of a semantic version it raises.

pairs.left: A fix that changes nothing callers rely on
A new feature that breaks nothing
A change that may break callers

prompt: A copy of shipquote that nobody built answers /version with the word ___ .
Put the stages of a delivery pipeline in order.
items: Deploy the same artifact to production
trap: The gate comes after staging: the decision is about an artifact already proved deployable.

prompt: What should a production deploy teach the team, ideally?

choices.text: Nothing new, only a confirmation
choices.why: Right. Same artifact, same command, same smoke test, different configuration.

choices.text: Whether the unit tests pass
choices.why: They ran stages ago.

choices.text: Whether the artifact can be built
choices.why: It was built once, at the start.

choices.text: How users react to a broken release
choices.why: That is what the earlier stages exist to prevent.

prompt: This repository's release workflow has no staging environment. Which of its jobs is the closest thing to a gate?

choices.text: Deploy, because it moves the service
choices.why: Deploy is what the gate would protect.

choices.text: Publish, because it creates the release
choices.why: Publish builds; it decides nothing.

choices.text: Tag and Checks, refusing up front
choices.why: Right. Its gate is a set of rules, not a person.

choices.text: None; it has no checks
choices.why: It calls the whole CI workflow.

prompt: Why does deploy.sh unpack each release into its own directory and switch a link?

choices.text: To save disk space
choices.why: It uses more space, keeping old releases.

choices.text: It changes in one step and keeps the old one
choices.why: Right. No half-old, half-new moment, and going back is another switch.

choices.text: Because tar cannot overwrite files
choices.why: It can; that is the risk being avoided.

choices.text: So staging and production share one directory
choices.why: Each environment has its own.

prompt: On which port did staging answer?
What does deploy.sh do when an environment has no config.env?

choices.text: Uses port 8080 by default
choices.why: No defaults: a guessed port is how production gets the wrong one.

choices.text: Copies staging's configuration
choices.why: Environments never borrow each other's settings.

choices.text: Stops with an error
choices.why: Right. It refuses before touching anything.

choices.text: Creates an empty one and continues
choices.why: That would start with no port at all.

prompt: Which two questions does shipquote's smoke test ask?

choices.text: Do the unit tests pass, and is coverage above 80%?
choices.why: Those are earlier stages.

choices.text: Is it up, and is it the version we meant?
choices.why: Right. /health and /version.

choices.text: Is the database migrated, and is the cache warm?
choices.why: Neither is asked by this script.

choices.text: Are users happy, and is latency low?
choices.why: That is watching production, lessons 10 and 11.

prompt: The preview deploy failed. What was wrong?

choices.text: The artifact's hash did not match
choices.why: That check passed; the process started.

choices.text: The port was 84OO, with letters
choices.why: Right. int() refused it and the process died.

choices.text: The version was dev
choices.why: The artifact was 1.4.0.

choices.text: Staging was already using the port
choices.why: Staging used 8200.

prompt: Why does the lesson call the smoke test the test of code that only runs in a deployment?

choices.text: Because the unit tests are deleted before deploying
choices.why: They stay; they just never run main().

choices.text: It runs main() with the real configuration
choices.why: Right. Lesson 4 left main() in the count for this reason.

choices.text: Because it is written in shell, not Python
choices.why: The language is not the point.

choices.text: Because it covers every route of the API
choices.why: It asks two.

prompt: Which of these belong in a smoke test run against production? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Asking /health
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: One real quote for a known CEP
choices.why: Right. It proves the main path works, not only that the process answers.

choices.text: Placing a test order that e-mails a customer
choices.why: Nothing that writes data a customer could see.

choices.text: A paid call to the carrier
choices.why: Nothing that costs money.

prompt: The artifact copied to /tmp had one byte added. What did deploy.sh do?

choices.text: Deployed it, since the name was right
choices.why: The name is not what is checked.

choices.text: Refused it; the SHA-256 was wrong
choices.why: Right. Before unpacking anything, with exit status 1.

choices.text: Rebuilt it from the commit
choices.why: Deploys never build.

choices.text: Deployed it and failed the smoke test
choices.why: It never got that far.

prompt: When is a person at the gate worth having, by the lesson?

choices.text: Always, because people are more careful than pipelines
choices.why: An approval always given is a delay.

choices.text: Never, because every gate should be automatic
choices.why: Some knowledge is not in the pipeline yet.

choices.text: When they know something the pipeline does not
choices.why: Right. A campaign in an hour, a carrier migrating tonight.

choices.text: When the tests are flaky
choices.why: Flaky tests are fixed, not supervised.

prompt: In GitHub Actions, a job waits for approval when it declares ___ : production.
Which of these are reasons the lesson gives not to deploy every change automatically? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A mobile store reviews every release
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A named person must approve by contract
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The software runs on customers' devices
choices.why: Right. Nobody can roll back a device in somebody's pocket.

choices.text: The team uses Python
choices.why: The language has nothing to do with it.

prompt: A change must go live at 9:00 on Black Friday. What does the lesson suggest instead of deploying at 9:00?

choices.text: Freeze all deploys for the week
choices.why: A freeze makes releasing an event, the opposite of the goal.

choices.text: Deploy early behind a flag
choices.why: Right. Deploying and releasing become separate acts.

choices.text: Deploy at 8:59 and skip the smoke test
choices.why: That adds risk at the worst moment.

choices.text: Build the artifact at 9:00
choices.why: Building is the start of the pipeline, not a launch switch.

prompt: Which question does the lesson say settles whether a team has continuous delivery?

choices.text: Do we deploy more than once a day?
choices.why: Frequency is a choice, not the property.

choices.text: Could we release main right now?
choices.why: Right. Who presses the button is a separate choice.

choices.text: Do we use GitHub Actions or GitLab CI?
choices.why: Tools do not decide it.

choices.text: Is our coverage above a target?
choices.why: Lesson 4 argued against targets.

prompt: Why does renaming a column in the same release as the code break a rollback?

choices.text: Because rollbacks never touch the database
choices.why: That is exactly why the old code meets the new schema.

choices.text: Old code meets a missing column
choices.why: Right. Code can go back; the migrated data did not.

choices.text: Because SQLite cannot rename columns
choices.why: It can; the timing is the problem.

choices.text: Because the artifact's hash changes
choices.why: The artifact is unrelated to the schema state.

prompt: Order the expand-and-contract steps for renaming cents to price_cents.
trap: Reading the new column before it is backfilled would show empty prices for old rows.

prompt: During step 4, read the new column, a bad release is rolled back to step 2's code. Is that safe?

choices.text: Yes, because both columns are kept current
choices.why: Right. Step 2's code reads cents, which step 4 still writes.

choices.text: No, because cents was dropped in step 4
choices.why: cents is dropped only at the contract step.

choices.text: No, because rollbacks need a migration down
choices.why: This pattern exists so they do not.

choices.text: Only if the artifact is rebuilt
choices.why: Rollback reuses a previous artifact.

prompt: Match each check in the lab's delivery to the mistake it caught or would catch.

pairs.right: An artifact changed on its way
A port with a letter O in it
An untagged build passing for a release
A restart that left the old version running

prompt: A team rebuilds its artifact in the production job 'to be safe'. A dependency released an hour earlier has a bug. What happens?

choices.text: Staging caught it, since staging ran the tests
choices.why: Staging tested the earlier build, without the new dependency.

choices.text: Production runs a build nobody tested
choices.why: Right. Build once, promote the same bytes.

choices.text: The hash check refuses it
choices.why: A new build writes its own new hash.

choices.text: Nothing, since dependencies are pinned in the artifact
choices.why: The rebuild is what picks up the new release.

prompt: Expand and contract turned one column rename into how many releases?
